questions.q: What is the difference between a Key Vault "secret" and a Key Vault "key"?
options: There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
A secret is an arbitrary stored string value; a key is cryptographic material used for operations like signing without exposing the raw key
Keys are only used for TLS certificates
Secrets can only store passwords, never API keys
questions.explain: Secrets store arbitrary values like API keys or connection strings as-is, while keys are cryptographic material Key Vault uses to perform operations without ever revealing the raw key material.

questions.q: What happens when you update an existing secret's value in Key Vault?
options: The old value is permanently deleted and unrecoverable
Key Vault creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one
The secret's name is automatically changed
Key Vault requires deleting and recreating the entire vault
questions.explain: Key Vault automatically versions secrets on update, preserving an audit trail and allowing rollback to a previous version rather than silently overwriting it.

questions.q: Why does Key Vault hide a secret's value behind a "Show Secret Value" button by default?
options: It's a cosmetic UI choice with no security purpose
So that viewing the actual value is a distinct, auditable action separate from merely seeing that the secret exists
Because secret values cannot be displayed in the Azure portal at all
To prevent the secret from ever being read programmatically
questions.explain: The extra click lets Key Vault's diagnostic logs distinguish "listed this secret" from "retrieved its value," which is important when investigating whether a credential was actually exposed.

questions.q: What Azure RBAC role is needed to read a secret's value from a specific Key Vault?
options: Global Administrator
Key Vault Secrets User, scoped to that vault
Any Reader role at the subscription level
No role is required — Key Vault secrets are publicly readable by default
questions.explain: Reading secret values requires a role like Key Vault Secrets User, scoped to the specific vault — the same role pattern used in Lesson 9's workload identity example.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect Key Vault access back to earlier lessons in the course?
options: It doesn't — Key Vault access is a completely separate system from Azure RBAC
Key Vault access is governed by the same Azure RBAC model from Lesson 6, and the Key Vault Secrets User role is the exact role federated in Lesson 9's workload identity example
Key Vault only supports the legacy access-policy model, never RBAC
Key Vault access requires a separate AWS IAM role
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties Key Vault's RBAC-based access control back to Lesson 6 (Azure RBAC) and Lesson 9 (workload identity), showing identity, RBAC, and secrets management as one connected design.
